title: IB Computer Science Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Computer Science exam technique for November: understand each paper, budget time by marks, trace code accurately and write stronger answers.
body_markdown:
Three weeks before the November session, revision can feel strangely productive. Notes become neater. Flashcards multiply. Yet the unanswered question remains: can you convert what you know into marks under timed conditions?


Effective **IB Computer Science exam technique** means matching time and detail to the marks, responding precisely to command terms, tracing algorithms by hand and practising the correct paper for your level and option. For November 2026 candidates, that means the syllabus first assessed in 2014 and examined for the final time in 2026, not the redesigned course beginning assessment in 2027.


This guide follows a hypothetical student through the final three weeks. The goal is not to learn everything again. It is to make existing knowledge usable.


### Your three-week checklist


- Confirm whether you are sitting SL or HL and identify your Paper 2 option.
- Learn each paper's duration, sections and available marks.
- Practise command terms rather than merely rereading content.
- Trace pseudocode and algorithms on paper every day.
- Allocate time broadly in proportion to marks.
- Review errors by type: knowledge, interpretation, logic or timing.
- Finish with timed papers in Exam mode.


### Three weeks out: understand what each paper demands


Our student begins by writing the assessment structure on one page. That simple act matters because Paper 1, Paper 2 and the HL-only Paper 3 reward different kinds of preparation.


The following structure applies to the course ending with the 2026 examination cycle. Always confirm arrangements and permitted materials with your school and current IB documentation.


Paper Level Time Marks Main focus


Paper 1 SL 1 hour 30 minutes 70 Compulsory short and structured questions on the SL core


Paper 1 HL 2 hours 10 minutes 100 Compulsory questions on the core and HL extension


Paper 2 SL 1 hour 45 Compulsory questions on one studied option


Paper 2 HL 1 hour 20 minutes 65 Compulsory questions on one studied option, including additional HL material


Paper 3 HL only 1 hour 30 Four compulsory questions based on a pre-seen case study


The options for Paper 2 are databases, modelling and simulation, web science, and object-oriented programming. You answer the option taught by your school. Revising all four wastes time that should be spent mastering one.


A useful starting point is RevisionDojo's broader guide to[getting a 7 in IB Computer Science](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-computer-science) , followed by a more focused[November mock-exam preparation plan](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-computer-science-mock-exam-prep-november) .


### Paper 1: turn knowledge into visible reasoning


Paper 1 contains compulsory questions. There is no strategic choice of sections, so the central skill is movement: collect accessible marks, recognise when a question is consuming too much time and return later if necessary.


A practical budget is close to one minute per mark. It is not a law. Reading, checking and longer algorithm questions distort the ratio slightly. Still, marks are the best available signal of expected depth. Spending eight minutes polishing a two-mark definition is usually a poor trade.


### Short responses and command terms


For **state** , give the requested fact without an essay. For **describe** , provide relevant characteristics or an account. For **explain** , connect a cause to an effect. For **compare** , address both items through corresponding similarities or differences.


Consider a question asking why cache improves performance. Naming cache is not an explanation. A stronger response establishes the chain: frequently required data or instructions can be held in faster memory close to the processor, reducing slower memory access and therefore reducing average retrieval time.


Use the marks as a clue. A three-mark question often needs several distinct, relevant points or a developed logical chain. Marks are awarded for creditworthy content, not answer length.


### Pseudocode, tracing and algorithms


When tracing code, do not simulate it mentally. Create a table showing variables, loop iterations and output. Update values in execution order, especially where one assignment depends on an earlier assignment in the same iteration.


For algorithm construction:


- initialise variables explicitly;
- use clear loop bounds and conditions;
- distinguish assignment from comparison;
- handle empty inputs and boundary values where relevant;
- return or output exactly what the question requests;
- dry-run the solution with a small example.


RevisionDojo's explanation of[computational thinking in IB Computer Science](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-computational-thinking-in-ib-computer-science) helps connect decomposition and abstraction to these questions. The[Computer Science last-minute study plan](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-study-ib-computer-science-if-you-left-it-until-the-last-minute) also identifies tracing, searching and sorting as useful high-yield practice areas.


A student calmly traces code while a giant figure asks whether the student can trace their panic


### Two weeks out: make Paper 2 option knowledge usable


By the second week, our student stops treating Paper 2 as a collection of definitions. Option questions test whether concepts can be applied to a stated system or problem.


Build a one-page map for your option. Include essential terminology, processes, advantages and limitations, common representations, and any algorithms or technical conventions in the guide. Then practise retrieving that material through questions rather than copying it again.


If you study object-oriented programming, trace object state carefully and distinguish a class from an instance. Track parameters, return values, inheritance and method calls. If you study databases, keep entities, attributes, keys, relationships and normalization reasoning distinct. For web science, connect technical mechanisms to implications in the given context. For modelling and simulation, explain assumptions, simplifications, validation and limitations rather than claiming that a model perfectly reproduces reality.


The pattern is consistent: identify the concept, apply it to the scenario, then explain the consequence. Generic knowledge earns less than relevant knowledge.


Use RevisionDojo's **Study Notes** and **Flashcards** to repair gaps, then move into the **Questionbank** . If an explanation remains unclear, **AI Chat** can help unpack it, while **Grading tools** can expose where a response lacks precision. The important transition is from recognition to production. Seeing a correct answer is not the same as being able to write one.


### HL Paper 3: treat the case study as a map, not a script


HL students face Paper 3, based on the pre-seen case study. Advance access creates an unusual temptation: predict exact questions and memorize prepared paragraphs. That feels safe but becomes fragile when the examination changes the angle.


Instead, annotate the case study in layers:


- define every technical term;
- map systems, actors, data and processes;
- identify benefits, risks, constraints and decisions;
- connect each issue to relevant syllabus concepts;
- research unfamiliar technologies sufficiently to explain them accurately;
- practise applying knowledge to altered scenarios.


Paper 3 has four compulsory questions worth 30 marks in one hour. Reserve time for the higher-mark evaluative response. Evaluation requires a reasoned judgment, not a list of advantages and disadvantages. Establish criteria, consider competing perspectives, use the case-study context and reach a qualified conclusion.


RevisionDojo's[guide to mastering IB Computer Science assessments](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/mastering-ib-computer-science-assessments) can help HL students combine content review with targeted question practice.


### The final week: rehearse decisions under pressure


With seven days left, our student changes the unit of revision. It is no longer chapters completed. It is decisions improved.


Complete timed sections before attempting full simulations. After each session, classify every lost mark:


Error type Corrective action


Knowledge gap Review the exact syllabus point with Study Notes and Flashcards


Misread command term Rewrite the response using the required task


Weak application Add details from the scenario or case study


Algorithm error Trace the logic with a table and test boundary cases


Timing problem Set a mark-based limit and move on when it expires


Vague expression Compare the response with the marking logic and make each point explicit


This is more useful than recording only a score. A score describes the attempt; an error log improves the next one.


RevisionDojo's[Computer Science time-management guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-practice-time-management-during-ib-computer-science-exams) develops the mark-based pacing method. If time has become genuinely tight, use the[one-week Computer Science revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-pass-ib-computer-science-in-1-week-last-minute-study-guide) to prioritise rather than panic.


### Exam-day technique for the November session


Read every question for its command term, subject and scope. Underline constraints such as “one,” “two,” “other than” or “with reference to the case study.” These small words often determine whether a knowledgeable answer is relevant.


Write distinct points distinctly. For longer answers, use brief paragraphs that each advance one part of the reasoning. If you become stuck, leave space and continue. A difficult three-mark question should not consume the time needed for an accessible eight-mark response.


For code and pseudocode, keep your work legible. Even when a final result is wrong, clearly expressed intermediate logic may contain creditworthy steps. Before time ends, check unanswered parts, loop boundaries, variable updates and whether extended responses reached an actual judgment.


The final three weeks are not about heroic study hours. They are about shortening the distance between understanding and execution. RevisionDojo brings that process together through its Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, Grading tools, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, Coursework Library and Tutors. Start with targeted practice in the **Questionbank** , then sit timed papers in **Exam mode** . That is where knowledge learns to survive the clock.
